newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Holderbank takes extra provisions in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Holderbank takes extra provisions in 1996.

text.p: Holderbank Financiere Glarus AG, the world's leading cement producer, said it was taking extraordinary provisions and valuation adjustments totalling 607 million Swiss francs on its 1996 accounts.
"Group net income (profit) after taxes is thereby reduced by 450 million Swiss francs to 196 million Swiss francs," Holderbank said in a statement on its 1996 results.
Holderbank, which also makes cement, clinker and aggregates, said the extraordinary provisions were taken in order to scale down capacity and to cover heightened business risk.
"The specific provisions and valuation adjustments are an extension of the restructurings already announced for Switzerland, Germany, France, Canada and Australia," it said.
The European cement market in particular was saturated at a low level after earlier boom years, it said.
In Switzerland, Holderbank said subsidiary HCB would close its Rekingen cement plant at the start of 1998.

Holderbank said the 1996 extraordinary provisions and value adjustments, together with previously announced measures, would allow it to cut fixed costs by a sustainable 50 million Swiss francs a year.
"To ensure cost leadership pursuant to our strategy, structurally induced capacity reduction is required," Holderbank said.

But Holderbank said it would still be able to serve European markets optimally even after shrinking capacity because of a "uniquely dense network of production locations", both wholly owned and through minorities in several European companies.
In Switzerland, Holderbank said it needed to cut domestic capacity due to rising cement imports, a lack of infrastructure projects, industrial overcapacity and declining home construction.
Rekingen, with a workforce of 100, is one of four HCB plants which together with another Holderbank factory in Switzerland have an annual cement capacity of about three million tonnes.
That contrasts with projected Swiss domestic demand of only 3.5 million tonnes or less a year by the year 2000, as compared to 5.5 million tonnes in 1990, the company said.
